0.0.n: Highlights Taiwanese people as a particular example.

0.2.n: 台湾 is Taiwan; 人 adds the sense of people from that place.

0.3.n: Marks Taiwanese people as the topic, continued in the next line.

1.0.n: Combines with ご飯 to make 朝ご飯, breakfast.

1.1.n: ご飯 can mean rice or a meal; here it forms 朝ご飯, breakfast.

1.2.n: Marks 朝ご飯 as the thing liked with 好き.

1.3.n: 好き describes a feeling of liking; it is not a verb in Japanese.

1.4.n: Connects 好き to the explanatory んです ending.

1.5.n: Short for の, adding an explanatory tone before です.

1.6.n: Makes the explanation polite rather than adding a separate action.

1.7.n: Emphasizes information the speaker is telling the listener.

2.0.n: Describes how frequently they buy and eat breakfast outside.

2.1.n: Here it suggests getting breakfast away from home.

2.2.n: Marks 外 as the place where the action happens.

2.3.n: Combines with ご飯 to form the word for breakfast.

2.4.n: Part of 朝ご飯 here, so it refers to breakfast rather than rice alone.

2.5.n: Marks 朝ご飯 as what they buy and eat.

2.6.n: The て-form of 買う connects buying to the next action, eating.

2.7.n: Polite form of 食べる; with よく, it describes a regular habit.

3.0.n: The speaker now introduces their own preference.

3.1.n: Marks 私 as the topic of the sentence continuing into the next line.

3.3.n: The name of a Taiwanese egg crepe, written in katakana.

3.4.n: Introduces a name and connects it to the description in the next line.

4.0.n: A place name modifying 朝ご飯 through の.

4.1.n: Links Taiwan to breakfast, indicating its origin or association.

4.2.n: Joins ご飯 to make 朝ご飯, breakfast.

4.3.n: Here 朝ご飯 refers to a breakfast food, namely danbing.

4.4.n: Marks the Taiwanese breakfast food as the thing the speaker likes.

4.5.n: 大 strengthens 好き to express a very strong liking.

4.6.n: Politely completes the statement of the speaker’s preference.

5.0.n: A place name identifying where the speaker was.

5.1.n: Marks the location of the speaker’s presence with いた.

5.2.n: Plain past form of いる, used for a person being somewhere.

5.3.n: Follows いた to indicate the time when the speaker was in Taiwan.

5.4.n: Makes the whole phrase 台湾にいた時 the time frame for what follows.

6.0.n: States the frequency directly, without needing a particle here.

6.1.n: This subtitle segment is only the beginning of the food name ダンピン, not a separate Japanese word.

6.2.n: Completes the food name ダンピン; read it together with ダン.

6.3.n: Marks ダンピン as the food the speaker ate.

6.4.n: Polite past of 食べている; 毎日 makes this a repeated past habit rather than one ongoing meal.

6.5.n: Adds a gentle, reflective tone as the speaker recalls that habit.

0.tip: は sets up a topic whose description comes in the next subtitle.

1.lit: Breakfast is liked, the thing is, you know.
1.tip: 好き uses が to mark the thing liked, rather than を.

2.lit: Often, outside, breakfast buy and eat.
2.tip: 買って links two actions in order: buying breakfast, then eating it.

3.tip: という connects the food’s name to 台湾の朝ご飯 in the next line.

4.tip: 大好き expresses a stronger preference than 好き: loving something rather than simply liking it.

5.lit: As for when I was in Taiwan,
5.tip: A plain past form can come before 時 even when the main sentence ends politely.

6.lit: Every day, danbing I was eating, you know.
6.tip: With 毎日, 食べていました describes a past habit, not just an action happening at one moment.
